title: Rescuing Your Pruning: Rethinking Visual Token Pruning and Post-Training Recovery in MLLMs

paper.title: Rescuing Your Pruning: Rethinking Visual Token Pruning and Post-Training Recovery in MLLMs
paper.abstract: Abstract Visual token pruning substantially reduces the inference cost of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet existing methods are mostly training-free and plug-and-play. They treat the resulting performance drop as an inevitable cost of compression and pursue increasingly complex pruning rules. We rethink this view through two questions: how much of the loss can post-training rescue, and, building on this recovery, how can joint compression push pruning to its limit? We curate a 282K-sample post-training mixture covering general VQA, reasoning, OCR, and grounding, and post-train 36 configurations that drop or merge tokens under a unified protocol. Post-training rescues most of the loss, even for OCR and grounding, and its adaptation gain in closing the gap between the pruned and the dense model grows as the budget tightens. For joint compression, we find that the vision encoder, not the LLM, dominates prefill time in native-resolution MLLMs, so where tokens are removed matters more than how many: keeping 40 % 40\% of tokens at the encoder runs faster than keeping 10 % 10\% at the projector. Our best configuration prunes the encoder lightly and the projector aggressively, leaves the LLM intact, and keeps general understanding and reasoning at the dense level. It accelerates the LLM stage by 3.49 × 3.49\times but the end-to-end time-to-first-token by only 1.54 × 1.54\times , showing that LLM-stage speedups overstate end-to-end gains. We hope these findings offer insights for future research on joint visual token compression. Our data, protocol, and code will be released.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Visual tokens, which often far outnumber text tokens, account for much of the inference cost of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), making visual token compression a primary route to acceleration [ 17 , 51 , 45 , 27 , 40 ] . Tokens can be reduced at three stages of the pipeline [ 46 ] : inside the vision encoder [ 3 , 16 ] , at the projector [ 1 , 59 , 50 ] , or within the LLM [ 4 , 49 , 8 ] , by either dropping or merging them, mostly as training-free modules [ 57 , 37 , 10 ] . Rethinking this practice raises two questions. First, how much of the accuracy lost to pruning can be recovered? As shown in Fig. 1 , training-free pruning largely preserves coarse-grained understanding but sharply degrades OCR and grounding, consistent with prior observations [ 9 , 7 , 14 ] . Yet lightweight post-training under the same pruning configuration pulls these nearly collapsed capabilities back to a large extent. Compression-aware post-training (CAPT) may thus mitigate the mismatch between the pruned input and a model trained on dense tokens [ 7 , 50 , 38 ] . Second, how should the three stages be compressed together? A single stage offers limited room for compression, and combining stages can remove more tokens, as recent pipelines that chain several stages have begun to show [ 28 , 12 , 61 ] . Joint compression, however, couples the stages, and losses across stages accumulate. Early pruning shortens later sequences, but differing stage costs mean fewer tokens need not reduce end-to-end latency. By adapting the model under joint pruning, CAPT can mitigate the accumulated mismatch and keep more aggressive combinations feasible. To study both questions systematically from the perspective of post-training, we first build a compact yet task-diverse training set of 282K samples, validate its composition through ablations, and check it for test contamination. Under a unified protocol that keeps every pruning rule unchanged, shown in Fig. 2 , we apply CAPT to 36 configurations: one dropping and one merging method at each stage, three keep ratios ( 40 % 40\% , 20 % 20\% , and 10 % 10\% ), and two backbones, Qwen2.5-VL-7B [ 36 ] and LLaVA-OneVision-1.5-8B [ 2 ] . We evaluate them on 12 benchmarks and report retention, the score relative to the unpruned model. Figure 1: Training-free vs. post-trained retention by capability. Results on Qwen2.5-VL-7B at 20 % 20\% keep, with each pruning level averaged over its dropping and merging methods. Arrows mark the gain from post-training, and the dashed line marks the dense model. CAPT improves every configuration and recovers most of the performance lost to pruning. At an average keep ratio of 20 % 20\% , it brings general understanding and reasoning close to the original model in nearly every configuration, and restores much of the OCR and grounding ability that training-free pruning nearly destroys. To trace where this recovery comes from, we take LLM-level pruning as a case study and contrast four training and evaluation states. They disentangle the pruning gap into a repairable adaptation mismatch and a residual of discarded evidence, and the post-training gain into a data gain and an adaptation gain. As the budget tightens, the residual grows, while the recovery relies increasingly on adapting to pruning. Visualizations further show that this adaptation acts on both sides of the pruning point. Upstream, the model learns features and attention that let the fixed rules select more relevant tokens. Downstream, the LLM learns to make better use of the few tokens that remain. CAPT also opens room for joint compression. With CAPT, joint configurations that keep only about 5 % 5\% to 7 % 7\% of the visual tokens still preserve the original model’s general understanding and reasoning, whereas recent training-free methods fall short of this level even at a 25 % 25\% budget. Exploring such configurations further leads to a more instructive finding: fewer tokens do not mean a faster model, and the configuration that keeps the fewest tokens is not the fastest. The question thus shifts from how many tokens to remove to where to remove them, and the answer depends on where the time goes. In native-resolution MLLMs such as Qwen2.5-VL, the encoder processes several times as many patches as the visual tokens the LLM receives after the projector’s compression, and such encoders typically run less efficiently than their FLOP count suggests. Most of the prefill time therefore goes to the vision encoder rather than the 7B LLM : 56.5 % 56.5\% in our setting, in line with the 40 % 40\% to over 80 % 80\% reported for similar models [ 60 , 26 , 42 , 5 ] . As a result, speedups measured inside the LLM overstate end-to-end gains . Prior work often reports speedups of 3 × 3\times or more at little accuracy cost, measured on the LLM stage or on LLaVA-style models whose light encoders add little latency [ 4 , 58 , 50 , 44 ] . On Qwen2.5-VL, keeping 10 % 10\% of the tokens at the projector speeds up the LLM stage by 3.38 × 3.38\times , yet the end-to-end time-to-first-token (TTFT) by only 1.38 × 1.38\times . 1 1 1 All methods are timed with one shared attention backend, PyTorch SDPA, as in prior work [ 16 , 55 ] . Real end-to-end speedups must therefore come from upstream, at the vision encoder and projector. Without training, however, upstream pruning sacrifices fine-grained capabilities. CAPT recovers them, making these extreme speedups feasible. Under the same quality requirement, our search yields three guidelines for joint compression. (1) If only one stage can be compressed, it should be the encoder. Keeping 40 % 40\% of the tokens at the encoder runs faster than keeping 10 % 10\% at the projector, because projector pruning leaves the encoder cost untouched and the LLM already approaches a length-independent fixed cost once about a hundred visual tokens remain (Appendix C.2 ). (2) If two stages can be compressed, light encoder pruning should be paired with aggressive projector pruning. Our fastest feasible configuration, ToMe-70 with AIM-10, speeds up the LLM stage by 3.49 × 3.49\times and TTFT by 1.54 × 1.54\times . (3) Compressing all three stages does not pay off. LLM pruning adds operator overhead, and its accuracy loss forces the encoder to keep more tokens, so the three-stage combination is slower than the best two-stage one and even slower than encoder pruning alone. Where tokens are removed thus matters more than how many are kept , which motivates accelerating the vision encoder itself in native-resolution MLLMs [ 5 , 42 , 41 ] . Our contributions are as follows: (1) Data and protocol. We build a compact, task-diverse post-training mixture and a unified protocol that apply to dropping and merging methods at all three stages. (2) Recoverability analysis. A large-scale evaluation shows that post-training substantially improves pruned models. The pruning-induced degradation can be decomposed into information loss and distribution mismatch, and post-training partly repairs the mismatch, with this adaptation becoming more important as the budget tightens. (3) Joint multi-stage compression. CAPT with joint compression makes extreme visual token compression feasible, accelerating LLM prefill by 3.49 × 3.49\times and TTFT by 1.54 × 1.54\times without degrading general understanding and reasoning. End-to-end measurements further show that where tokens are removed matters more than how many are kept, and that LLM-stage speedups overstate end-to-end gains. Figure 2: Overview of our unified framework. Pruning methods are organized by mechanism, dropping or merging, and by level, encoder, projector, or LLM. Post-training recovery is evaluated across General, Reasoning, OCR, and Grounding under single-stage and joint pruning configurations.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Visual token compression reduces the redundant visual sequence in MLLMs and has mainly developed along two directions: dropping and merging. Token dropping removes low-utility visual tokens by estimating token importance from attention patterns [ 4 , 49 , 52 ] or feature similarity [ 55 , 1 ] . FastV [ 4 ] , for example, prunes half of the visual tokens after the second LLM layer using the attention from the last text token to visual tokens. Token merging takes a softer route by fusing redundant token representations. AIM [ 59 ] directly merges similar token pairs, FiCoCo [ 12 ] recycles information by merging less important tokens into important retained tokens, and PACT [ 8 ] clusters similar tokens into compact representatives. Unlike most training-free or plug-and-play studies, we revisit dropping and merging from a post-training perspective, analyzing how these two mechanisms behave after adaptation. Efficient MLLM inference has motivated visual token compression beyond a single module, with recent methods combining reduction across multiple pipeline stages. FiCoCo [ 12 ] adopts an encoder–LLM pipeline with attention-guided pruning and information recycling, while FocusLLaVA [ 61 ] combines projector-level multi-scale sampling with LLM-level text-to-vision pruning. More recent methods extend compression to the encoder–projector–LLM pipeline: METEOR [ 28 ] integrates encoder pruning, cross-encoder redundancy removal, and instance-adaptive LLM pruning, and SAINT [ 16 ] applies similarity-aware pruning across stages. However, these methods mainly propose fixed multi-stage pipelines, leaving the interaction among stages and the allocation of compression budgets under the same final token budget insufficiently understood. We therefore systematically investigate joint encoder–projector–LLM compression and analyze how stage-wise budgets affect the accuracy–efficiency trade-off after adaptation.

sections.heading: Post-Training Data.
sections.text: Although some training-free pruning methods also report results with post-training, their data recipes always vary. We therefore first construct a unified, lightweight post-training dataset. Building upon the 133K LLaVA-Icons corpus [ 47 ] , a compact subset of LLaVA-665K [ 25 ] , we reorganize the originally multi-turn conversations into single-turn samples anchored by individual images. We then add small random portions of ChartQA [ 33 ] , DVQA [ 18 ] , AI2D [ 20 ] , DocVQA [ 34 ] , LLaVAR [ 56 ] , and TQA [ 21 ] , together with visual grounding data from LLaVA-665K, so that the mixture of about 282K samples covers general VQA, reasoning, OCR, and grounding. For visual grounding data used with Qwen-series models, we convert bounding boxes to normalized coordinates w.r.t. the original image resolution. Appendix A.1 details the dataset composition, Appendix A.2 reports train–test overlap statistics, and Appendix A.3 presents data ablations.

sections.heading: Training Protocol.
sections.text: Training-free pruning rules are designed for a frozen model, so we adapt them to CAPT under one uniform protocol. Pruning is a discrete operation defined by fixed arithmetic rather than learnable parameters, so we keep every rule exactly as specified and cut the gradient at the selection: what adapts is the model upstream and downstream of the pruning point, never the criterion itself. Pruning also reshapes the batch, since the number of surviving tokens varies across samples. We re-pack each sequence after every reduction, pad to the longest one in the batch, and extend the attention mask and labels so that padded positions enter neither attention nor the loss. For positions, retained tokens keep their pre-pruning indices and rotary embeddings are recomputed from those indices rather than the compacted ones, preserving the spatial layout of the dense model. We experiment on Qwen2.5-VL-7B [ 36 ] and LLaVA-OneVision-1.5-8B (LLaVA-OV-1.5-8B) [ 2 ] . LLM-level methods unfreeze only the language model. All other methods are trained with every module unfrozen. One setting deserves note: Qwen2.5-VL encodes images at dynamic resolution, so max_pixels strongly affects fine-grained detail and training cost, and we fix it to 451,584 451{,}584 as a balance between the two. The remaining configuration is shared across runs: one epoch over the corpus, a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 5 1\times 10^{-5} , bfloat16 precision, a maximum sequence length of 8192, and DeepSpeed ZeRO-2. Each run takes roughly four hours on 8 NVIDIA H20 80 GB GPUs.

sections.heading: Evaluation Protocol and Metrics.
sections.text: We evaluate four capability groups with lmms-eval [ 54 ] under identical settings for all models. General ability is measured on GQA [ 15 ] , VQA-v2 [ 11 ] , and OK-VQA [ 32 ] , and reasoning on ScienceQA [ 30 ] , AI2D [ 20 ] , and POPE [ 23 ] , the last of which probes object-hallucination reasoning. OCR ability is measured on TextVQA [ 39 ] , DocVQA [ 34 ] , and OCRBench [ 29 ] , and grounding on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ [ 19 , 53 ] , and RefCOCOg [ 31 ] . We report ANLS for DocVQA and Acc@0.5 for grounding, where RefCOCO and RefCOCO+ are averaged over testA and testB and RefCOCOg uses its test split. All other benchmarks report accuracy. To summarize performance under pruning, we report two retention metrics relative to the dense base model. The retention of a task is the pruned-model score divided by the dense-model score, expressed as a percentage. We first average retention within each group and then across groups. General-Reasoning Retention (GRR) averages the General and Reasoning groups, and All-Task Retention (ATR) averages all four groups.

sections.heading: Latency Measurement.
sections.text: All latency measurements use a single NVIDIA A100 GPU with batch size 1, SDPA attention, and the evaluation resolution, where max_pixels is set to 1,605,632 1{,}605{,}632 . We report TTFT, measured with a single generated token, together with its breakdown into the vision encoder, the projector, and the LLM. Each number is averaged over 5,000 5{,}000 TextVQA samples after five warm-up samples.

sections.heading: 4 Rescuing Pruning Across Levels and Mechanisms
sections.text: To systematically investigate the effectiveness of post-training across pruning methods, we comprehensively explore three dimensions: the pruning mechanism (dropping vs. merging), the pruning position (encoder, projector, and LLM), and the compression strength ( 40 / 20 / 10 % 40/20/10\% ). To account for dynamic-resolution inputs and reflect the actual computational budget, we use the average visual-token keep ratio per LLM layer as the invariant for all comparisons. Table 1 summarizes the main results under encoder- and projector-level pruning, and Appendices F.1 , F.2 , and F.3 give the full results for each level.

Section 4.2 decomposes this gap using LLM-level pruning as a case study. The pruning mechanism reveals a different pattern. Dropping removes selected tokens entirely, whereas merging aggregates them into the surviving tokens and therefore preserves a compressed, albeit distorted, representation of the original visual evidence. Under training-free pruning, merging often shows a clear advantage, especially at aggressive compression. After CAPT, however, this advantage largely disappears at the encoder and projector levels, where matched dropping–merging pairs differ by at most 1.4 1.4 ATR points on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and dropping can even perform slightly better, as SAINT reaches 80.3 80.3 against 78.9 78.9 for ToMe at 10 % 10\% keep. These results suggest that post-training can largely adapt to the representation distortion introduced by merging, causing much of its training-free advantage to vanish at earlier stages. When compression becomes more aggressive and is applied inside the LLM, however, preserving visual evidence remains important, whereas information discarded by dropping cannot be recovered through adaptation. The overall recovery trend is consistent across the two backbones, although its magnitude is backbone-dependent. One caveat concerns grounding on LLaVA-OV-1.5-8B: after post-training, the dense model itself reaches 150.3 150.3 retention relative to the Dense-Free baseline, indicating that the original model is substantially under-trained for grounding. Consequently, post-pruning grounding scores above 100 100 on this backbone should not be interpreted as outperforming the corresponding adapted dense model. sections.heading: 4.2 Where Does the Recovery Come From?
sections.text: The previous results show that post-training can recover a large fraction of the performance lost to visual-token pruning. Yet aggressively pruned models often remain below the dense reference even after training. This suggests a natural decomposition of the pruning-induced performance gap into two parts: a recoverable component that can be restored through post-training, and a residual component that mainly reflects the information loss inevitably introduced by pruning. We write Δ gap = G recoverable + R res . \Delta_{\mathrm{gap}}=G_{\mathrm{recoverable}}+R_{\mathrm{res}}. (1) The recoverable component requires further attribution. Our post-training uses a small and diverse dataset to adapt the upstream and downstream layers of the pruning operation to the compressed token distribution, thereby mitigating pruning-induced mismatches such as the attention gap. However, introducing post-training data inevitably brings an additional source of performance gain that is independent of pruning adaptation. We therefore further decompose the recoverable gain into a data gain and an adaptation gain : G recoverable = G data + G adapt . G_{\mathrm{recoverable}}=G_{\mathrm{data}}+G_{\mathrm{adapt}}. sections.heading: Aggressive pruning makes recovery more adaptation-dependent and more information-limited.
sections.text: Under aggressive budgets, G adapt G_{\mathrm{adapt}} exceeds G data G_{\mathrm{data}} in ATR and accounts for over 60 % 60\% of the recoverable gain at 10 % 10\% keep, showing that the benefit of CAPT does not come merely from the additional data. Once information loss becomes severe, however, adaptation reaches a ceiling. G adapt G_{\mathrm{adapt}} stays nearly flat between 20 % 20\% and 10 % 10\% keep, while the residual keeps growing and more than doubles for PDrop on Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Since Prune-aware and Dense-PT use the same data and training recipe and differ only in whether pruning is applied, this uncompensated gap mainly stems from information loss and concentrates on fine-grained tasks.

sections.heading: CAPT rescues representation mismatch, but not discarded evidence.
sections.text: Dropping removes tokens outright, along with the information they carry. Merging instead aggregates this information into the retained tokens, at the cost of perturbing the original representations. Post-training adapts to this perturbation and lets the extra information kept by merging take effect. At 10 % 10\% keep, PACT and PDrop gain comparably from adaptation, yet PACT leaves a residual that is one fifth to one third smaller and outperforms PDrop by 12.5 12.5 and 9.6 9.6 points in ATR on the two backbones. Post-training thus determines how well the model exploits the compressed representation, while the information preserved by pruning sets the ceiling of recovery. To qualitatively examine how post-training changes the pruned representation, we visualize the retained tokens and text-to-vision attention for all six methods at 20 % 20\% keep on a RefCOCO grounding example in Fig. 4 . Upstream of the pruning point, post-training reshapes the feature and attention distributions that the pruning rules operate on, so that the rules select tokens more effectively and more retained visual tokens fall inside the ground-truth region. Downstream, the LLM assigns stronger relative attention to the retained tokens within the target region, indicating that it learns to exploit the remaining visual evidence more effectively. Together, these two effects constitute the adaptation gain quantified above.

sections.heading: 5 How Far Can Post-Training Push Pruning?
sections.text: Having established that post-training substantially improves the tolerance of MLLMs to aggressive visual-token pruning, we ask how much prefill speedup can be achieved while general understanding and reasoning remain essentially lossless. Under the latency setting of Section 3 , dense Qwen2.5-VL-7B takes 213.06 213.06 ms TTFT per sample, of which the vision encoder accounts for 120.43 120.43 ms, the projector for 0.65 0.65 ms, and the LLM for 85.10 85.10 ms. The projector itself is almost free, yet it is a natural compression point, because pruning there shortens the visual sequence processed by the entire LLM. Projector-level pruning also preserves quality at aggressive budgets. As shown in Section 4.1 , at 10 % 10\% keep on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, post-trained encoder-level ToMe retains only 78.9 78.9 ATR, whereas projector-level AIM retains 89.5 89.5 . We therefore fix AIM at 10 % 10\% keep, denoted AIM-10, as a projector anchor and search how much additional compression the encoder and the LLM can absorb on top of it. Figure 5: Multi-level compression search with post-training. AIM is fixed at 10 % 10\% keep at the projector. (a) Encoder-level ToMe with a dense LLM. (b) LLM-level PACT with a dense encoder. (c) LLM-level PDrop and (d) LLM-level PACT with ToMe fixed at 80 % 80\% . Blue circles and red squares denote GRR and ATR, dashed lines mark the constraints GRR = 100 \mathrm{GRR}=100 and ATR = 85 \mathrm{ATR}=85 , and highlighted points mark the lowest feasible keep ratio. At the encoder we use ToMe, which matches SAINT in latency but performs better, as compared in Appendix C.1 . To locate the compression limit of each level under essentially lossless performance, we search over keep ratios subject to a quality constraint. We require GRR to stay at or above 100 100 , i.e., general understanding and reasoning at roughly the dense level, and ATR to stay at or above 85 85 , and we select the lowest keep ratio that satisfies both, as shown in Fig. 5 . With additional compression at a single level, the encoder can be pushed to ToMe-70 and the LLM to PACT-50. To also reduce the encoder, which dominates latency, we further combine all three levels. Since losses accumulate across levels, each level must retain more tokens when combined, and the feasible three-level configuration becomes ToMe-80, AIM-10, and PACT-70. Because the clustering and merging of PACT introduce extra overhead, we also try replacing it with the lighter PDrop. Under the same combination, however, PDrop fails to satisfy the constraint even at 90 % 90\% keep, indicating that the information discarded by dropping becomes increasingly intolerable near the compression limit and that preserving visual evidence matters more. CAPT remains effective for such multi-level joint pruning, keeping these aggressive combinations within the feasible region. Fig. 5 , however, only locates this frontier in token space. Pruning at different levels removes different amounts of computation and introduces different operator costs. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: This paper revisits visual token compression in multimodal large language models from the perspective of post-training. We point out that the performance degradation after pruning stems not only from unrecoverable information loss, but also from the adaptation gap between compressed visual tokens and the original dense-token distribution. To this end, we establish a unified compression-aware post-training framework and systematically analyze the recovery behavior of different compression mechanisms at the encoder, projector, and LLM levels. Our framework achieves significant and comprehensive performance recovery across diverse pruning settings, suggesting that a substantial portion of the degradation caused by training-free pruning is adaptable. Furthermore, we explore aggressive joint pruning across levels, which, with compression-aware post-training, attains the highest speedup among nearly lossless configurations.

To explain this, we vary only the number of tokens N N entering the LLM, using dense Qwen2.5-VL-7B and projector-level AIM at 40 40 , 20 20 , 10 10 , and 7 % 7\% keep, and fit the LLM prefill latency as t LLM = a + b ​ N t_{\mathrm{LLM}}=a+bN , as shown in Fig. 6 . Once the LLM approaches its floor, token count is no longer a reliable proxy for latency.

sections.heading: Appendix D Details of Pruning Methods
sections.text: We study one dropping and one merging method at each pruning level: SAINT and ToMe at the vision encoder, DivPrune and AIM at the projector, and PDrop and PACT inside the LLM.

sections.heading: SAINT [ 16 ] .
sections.text: SAINT can be applied in a training-free manner to prune visual tokens by estimating token redundancy from key-embedding similarity graphs and using layer-adaptive pruning rates across the multimodal pipeline.

sections.heading: ToMe [ 3 ] .
sections.text: ToMe is a training-free token merging method that accelerates Vision Transformers by iteratively matching similar tokens and merging them in pairs inside transformer blocks, thereby reducing token redundancy without additional training.

sections.heading: DivPrune [ 1 ] .
sections.text: DivPrune reduces visual tokens by formulating pruning as a Max-Min Diversity Problem, retaining a diverse subset of tokens while removing visually redundant or less informative ones.

sections.heading: AIM [ 59 ] .
sections.text: AIM improves multimodal inference efficiency by first merging similar visual tokens before the LLM and then progressively pruning less important visual tokens inside LLM layers.

sections.heading: PyramidDrop (PDrop) [ 49 ] .
sections.text: PyramidDrop progressively reduces visual tokens across transformer layers with a pyramid-like schedule, removing more tokens in earlier stages while preserving more tokens in later layers.

sections.heading: PACT [ 8 ] .
sections.text: PACT reduces visual tokens by pruning less informative tokens and clustering nearby redundant tokens into representative embeddings.

sections.heading: COCO [ 24 ] .
sections.text: COCO is a large-scale dataset of natural images with rich object, segmentation, and caption annotations, widely used for image captioning and general visual understanding.

sections.heading: VG [ 22 ] .
sections.text: Visual Genome (VG) provides dense annotations of objects, attributes, and relationships grounded in image regions, supporting fine-grained scene understanding and region-level visual grounding.

sections.heading: OCRVQA [ 35 ] .
sections.text: OCR-VQA consists of book cover images paired with questions about titles, authors, and other textual content, requiring joint OCR and visual question answering.

sections.heading: ChartQA [ 33 ] .
sections.text: ChartQA evaluates question answering over chart images, requiring both visual perception of chart elements and logical or arithmetic reasoning over the underlying data.

sections.heading: DVQA [ 18 ] .
sections.text: DVQA evaluates understanding of bar charts through questions about structure, data retrieval, and reasoning, with answers often containing chart-specific vocabulary.

sections.heading: LLaVAR [ 56 ] .
sections.text: LLaVAR augments visual instruction tuning with text-rich images, enhancing the ability of multimodal models to read and reason over textual content embedded in images.

sections.heading: TQA [ 21 ] .
sections.text: TQA (Textbook Question Answering) evaluates multimodal reasoning over middle-school science textbooks, combining text passages, diagrams, and questions that require contextual understanding.

sections.heading: ShareGPT [ 6 ] .
sections.text: ShareGPT is a collection of user-shared conversations with ChatGPT, commonly used as a language-only instruction-following corpus to preserve linguistic capability during multimodal fine-tuning.

sections.heading: GQA [ 15 ] .
sections.text: GQA evaluates compositional visual reasoning based on scene-graph annotations from Visual Genome.

sections.heading: VQA-v2 [ 11 ] .
sections.text: VQA-v2 is a balanced open-ended visual question answering benchmark designed to reduce language priors and encourage visual grounding.

sections.heading: OK-VQA [ 32 ] .
sections.text: OK-VQA evaluates knowledge-based visual question answering, where answering often requires external or commonsense knowledge beyond the image content.

sections.heading: ScienceQA [ 30 ] .
sections.text: ScienceQA evaluates multimodal scientific reasoning over questions from natural, language, and social sciences, where the image-based subset requires models to reason over visual inputs.

sections.heading: AI2D [ 20 ] .
sections.text: AI2D evaluates diagram understanding, requiring models to interpret labels, symbols, visual structures, and spatial relations.

sections.heading: POPE [ 23 ] .
sections.text: POPE is a diagnostic benchmark for object hallucination, using binary questions to test whether models falsely report nonexistent objects.

sections.heading: TextVQA [ 39 ] .
sections.text: TextVQA evaluates scene-text understanding by requiring models to recognize and reason over text in natural images.

sections.heading: DocVQA [ 34 ] .
sections.text: DocVQA evaluates document image question answering, emphasizing OCR, layout understanding, and information localization.

sections.heading: OCRBench [ 29 ] .
sections.text: OCRBench evaluates OCR-related capabilities of MLLMs across text recognition, document understanding, information extraction, and related tasks.

sections.heading: RefCOCO [ 19 , 53 ] .
sections.text: RefCOCO evaluates referring expression comprehension by requiring models to localize objects described by natural-language expressions.

sections.heading: RefCOCO+ [ 19 , 53 ] .
sections.text: RefCOCO+ emphasizes appearance-based referring expressions with fewer absolute location cues, making it more dependent on fine-grained object attributes.

sections.heading: RefCOCOg [ 31 , 53 ] .
sections.text: RefCOCOg contains longer and more descriptive referring expressions, testing fine-grained and context-rich visual grounding.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.33688v1 [cs.CV] 24 Oct 2026 \tl_set:Ne \tcboxmath tcboxmath \tl_set:Ne \tcbhighmath tcbhighmath \authornotes * Equal contribution. † Corresponding author. \contact peiran.yin@sjtu.edu.cn xyshen@eitech.edu.cn Rescuing Your Pruning: Rethinking Visual Token Pruning and Post-Training Recovery in MLLMs Peiran Yin 1,2,* Hao Wu 1,2,* Zihao Yang 3 Haozhe Hu 1,2 Xudong Wang 1 Xiaoyu Shen 1,† Affiliation: 1 EIT-NLP Lab, Eastern Institute of Technology, Ningbo 2 Shanghai Jiao Tong University 3 Uppsala University Abstract Visual token pruning substantially reduces the inference cost of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet existing methods are mostly training-free and plug-and-play. They treat the resulting performance drop as an inevitable cost of compression and pursue increasingly complex pruning rules. We rethink this view through two questions: how much of the loss can post-training rescue, and, building on this recovery, how can joint compression push pruning to its limit? We curate a 282K-sample post-training mixture covering general VQA, reasoning, OCR, and grounding, and post-train 36 configurations that drop or merge tokens under a unified protocol. Post-training rescues most of the loss, even for OCR and grounding, and its adaptation gain in closing the gap between the pruned and the dense model grows as the budget tightens. For joint compression, we find that the vision encoder, not the LLM, dominates prefill time in native-resolution MLLMs, so where tokens are removed matters more than how many: keeping 40 % 40\% of tokens at the encoder runs faster than keeping 10 % 10\% at the projector. Our best configuration prunes the encoder lightly and the projector aggressively, leaves the LLM intact, and keeps general understanding and reasoning at the dense level. It accelerates the LLM stage by 3.49 × 3.49\times but the end-to-end time-to-first-token by only 1.54 × 1.54\times , showing that LLM-stage speedups overstate end-to-end gains. We hope these findings offer insights for future research on joint visual token compression. Our data, protocol, and code will be released. 1 Introduction Visual tokens, which often far outnumber text tokens, account for much of the inference cost of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), making visual token compression a primary route to acceleration [ 17 , 51 , 45 , 27 , 40 ] . Tokens can be reduced at three stages of the pipeline [ 46 ] : inside the vision encoder [ 3 , 16 ] , at the projector [ 1 , 59 , 50 ] , or within the LLM [ 4 , 49 , 8 ] , by either dropping or merging them, mostly as training-free modules [ 57 , 37 , 10 ] . Rethinking this practice raises two questions. First, how much of the accuracy lost to pruning can be recovered? As shown in Fig. 1 , training-free pruning largely preserves coarse-grained understanding but sharply degrades OCR and grounding, consistent with prior observations [ 9 , 7 , 14 ] . Yet lightweight post-training under the same pruning configuration pulls these nearly collapsed capabilities back to a large extent. Compression-aware post-training (CAPT) may thus mitigate the mismatch between the pruned input and a model trained on dense tokens [ 7 , 50 , 38 ] . Second, how should the three stages be compressed together? A single stage offers limited room for compression, and combining stages can remove more tokens, as recent pipelines that chain several stages have begun to show [ 28 , 12 , 61 ] . Joint compression, however, couples the stages, and losses across stages accumulate. Early pruning shortens later sequences, but differing stage costs mean fewer tokens need not reduce end-to-end latency. By adapting the model under joint pruning, CAPT can mitigate the accumulated mismatch and keep more aggressive combinations feasible. To study both questions systematically from the perspective of post-training, we first build a compact yet task-diverse training set of 282K samples, validate its composition through ablations, and check it for test contamination. Under a unified protocol that keeps every pruning rule unchanged, shown in Fig. 2 , we apply CAPT to 36 configurations: one dropping and one merging method at each stage, three keep ratios ( 40 % 40\% , 20 % 20\% , and 10 % 10\% ), and two backbones, Qwen2.5-VL-7B [ 36 ] and LLaVA-OneVision-1.5-8B [ 2 ] . We evaluate them on 12 benchmarks and report retention, the score relative to the unpruned model. Figure 1: Training-free vs. post-trained retention by capability. Results on Qwen2.5-VL-7B at 20 % 20\% keep, with each pruning level averaged over its dropping and merging methods. Arrows mark the gain from post-training, and the dashed line marks the dense model. CAPT improves every configuration and recovers most of the performance lost to pruning. At an average keep ratio of 20 % 20\% , it brings general understanding and reasoning close to the original model in nearly every configuration, and restores much of the OCR and grounding ability that training-free pruning nearly destroys. To trace where this recovery comes from, we take LLM-level pruning as a case study and contrast four training and evaluation states. They disentangle the pruning gap into a repairable adaptation mismatch and a residual of discarded evidence, and the post-training gain into a data gain and an adaptation gain. As the budget tightens, the residual grows, while the recovery relies increasingly on adapting to pruning. Visualizations further show that this adaptation acts on both sides of the pruning point. Upstream, the model learns features and attention that let the fixed rules select more relevant tokens. Downstream, the LLM learns to make better use of the few tokens that remain. CAPT also opens room for joint compression. With CAPT, joint configurations that keep only about 5 % 5\% to 7 % 7\% of the visual tokens still preserve the original model’s general understanding and reasoning, whereas recent training-free methods fall short of this level even at a 25 % 25\% budget. Exploring such configurations further leads to a more instructive finding: fewer tokens do not mean a faster model, and the configuration that keeps the fewest tokens is not the fastest. The question thus shifts from how many tokens to remove to where to remove them, and the answer depends on where the time goes. In native-resolution MLLMs such as Qwen2.5-VL, the encoder processes several times as many patches as the visual tokens the LLM receives after the projector’s compression, and such encoders typically run less efficiently than their FLOP count suggests. Most of the prefill time therefore goes to the vision encoder rather than the 7B LLM : 56.5 % 56.5\% in our setting, in line with the 40 % 40\% to over 80 % 80\% reported for similar models [ 60 , 26 , 42 , 5 ] . As a result, speedups measured inside the LLM overstate end-to-end gains . Prior work often reports speedups of 3 × 3\times or more at little accuracy cost, measured on the LLM stage or on LLaVA-style models whose light encoders add little latency [ 4 , 58 , 50 , 44 ] . On Qwen2.5-VL, keeping 10 % 10\% of the tokens at the projector speeds up the LLM stage by 3.38 × 3.38\times , yet the end-to-end time-to-first-token (TTFT) by only 1.38 × 1.38\times . 1 1 1 All methods are timed with one shared attention backend, PyTorch SDPA, as in prior work [ 16 , 55 ] . Real end-to-end speedups must therefore come from upstream, at the vision encoder and projector. Without training, however, upstream pruning sacrifices fine-grained capabilities. CAPT recovers them, making these extreme speedups feasible. Under the same quality requirement, our search yields three guidelines for joint compression. (1) If only one stage can be compressed, it should be the encoder. Keeping 40 % 40\% of the tokens at the encoder runs faster than keeping 10 % 10\% at the projector, because projector pruning leaves the encoder cost untouched and the LLM already approaches a length-independent fixed cost once about a hundred visual tokens remain (Appendix C.2 ). (2) If two stages can be compressed, light encoder pruning should be paired with aggressive projector pruning. Our fastest feasible configuration, ToMe-70 with AIM-10, speeds up the LLM stage by 3.49 × 3.49\times and TTFT by 1.54 × 1.54\times . (3) Compressing all three stages does not pay off. LLM pruning adds operator overhead, and its accuracy loss forces the encoder to keep more tokens, so the three-stage combination is slower than the best two-stage one and even slower than encoder pruning alone. Where tokens are removed thus matters more than how many are kept , which motivates accelerating the vision encoder itself in native-resolution MLLMs [ 5 , 42 , 41 ] . Our contributions are as follows: (1) Data and protocol. We build a compact, task-diverse post-training mixture and a unified protocol that apply to dropping and merging methods at all three stages. (2) Recoverability analysis. A large-scale evaluation shows that post-training substantially improves pruned models. The pruning-induced degradation can be decomposed into information loss and distribution mismatch, and post-training partly repairs the mismatch, with this adaptation becoming more important as the budget tightens. (3) Joint multi-stage compression. CAPT with joint compression makes extreme visual token compression feasible, accelerating LLM prefill by 3.49 × 3.49\times and TTFT by 1.54 × 1.54\times without degrading general understanding and reasoning. End-to-end measurements further show that where tokens are removed matters more than how many are kept, and that LLM-stage speedups overstate end-to-end gains. Figure 2: Overview of our unified framework. Pruning methods are organized by mechanism, dropping or merging, and by level, encoder, projector, or LLM. Post-training recovery is evaluated across General, Reasoning, OCR, and Grounding under single-stage and joint pruning configurations. 2 Related Work Visual token compression reduces the redundant visual sequence in MLLMs and has mainly developed along two directions: dropping and merging. Token dropping removes low-utility visual tokens by estimating token importance from attention patterns [ 4 , 49 , 52 ] or feature similarity [ 55 , 1 ] . FastV [ 4 ] , for example, prunes half of the visual tokens after the second LLM layer using the attention from the last text token to visual tokens. Token merging takes a softer route by fusing redundant token representations. AIM [ 59 ] directly merges similar token pairs, FiCoCo [ 12 ] recycles information by merging less important tokens into important retained tokens, and PACT [ 8 ] clusters similar tokens into compact representatives. Unlike most training-free or plug-and-play studies, we revisit dropping and merging from a post-training perspective, analyzing how these two mechanisms behave after adaptation. Efficient MLLM inference has motivated visual token compression beyond a single module, with recent methods combining reduction across multiple pipeline stages. FiCoCo [ 12 ] adopts an encoder–LLM pipeline with attention-guided pruning and information recycling, while FocusLLaVA [ 61 ] combines projector-level multi-scale sampling with LLM-level text-to-vision pruning. More recent methods extend compression to the encoder–projector–LLM pipeline: METEOR [ 28 ] integrates encoder pruning, cross-encoder redundancy removal, and instance-adaptive LLM pruning, and SAINT [ 16 ] applies similarity-aware pruning across stages. However, these methods mainly propose fixed multi-stage pipelines, leaving the interaction among stages and the allocation of compression budgets under the same final token budget insufficiently understood. We therefore systematically investigate joint encoder–projector–LLM compression and analyze how stage-wise budgets affect the accuracy–efficiency trade-off after adaptation. 3 Post-Training and Evaluation Post-Training Data. Although some training-free pruning methods also report results with post-training, their data recipes always vary. We therefore first construct a unified, lightweight post-training dataset. Building upon the 133K LLaVA-Icons corpus [ 47 ] , a compact subset of LLaVA-665K [ 25 ] , we reorganize the originally multi-turn conversations into single-turn samples anchored by individual images. We then add small random portions of ChartQA [ 33 ] , DVQA [ 18 ] , AI2D [ 20 ] , DocVQA [ 34 ] , LLaVAR [ 56 ] , and TQA [ 21 ] , together with visual grounding data from LLaVA-665K, so that the mixture of about 282K samples covers general VQA, reasoning, OCR, and grounding. For visual grounding data used with Qwen-series models, we convert bounding boxes to normalized coordinates w.r.t. the original image resolution. Appendix A.1 details the dataset composition, Appendix A.2 reports train–test overlap statistics, and Appendix A.3 presents data ablations. Training Protocol. Training-free pruning rules are designed for a frozen model, so we adapt them to CAPT under one uniform protocol. Pruning is a discrete operation defined by fixed arithmetic rather than learnable parameters, so we keep every rule exactly as specified and cut the gradient at the selection: what adapts is the model upstream and downstream of the pruning point, never the criterion itself. Pruning also reshapes the batch, since the number of surviving tokens varies across samples. We re-pack each sequence after every reduction, pad to the longest one in the batch, and extend the attention mask and labels so that padded positions enter neither attention nor the loss. For positions, retained tokens keep their pre-pruning indices and rotary embeddings are recomputed from those indices rather than the compacted ones, preserving the spatial layout of the dense model. We experiment on Qwen2.5-VL-7B [ 36 ] and LLaVA-OneVision-1.5-8B (LLaVA-OV-1.5-8B) [ 2 ] . LLM-level methods unfreeze only the language model. All other methods are trained with every module unfrozen. One setting deserves note: Qwen2.5-VL encodes images at dynamic resolution, so max_pixels strongly affects fine-grained detail and training cost, and we fix it to 451,584 451{,}584 as a balance between the two. The remaining configuration is shared across runs: one epoch over the corpus, a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 5 1\times 10^{-5} , bfloat16 precision, a maximum sequence length of 8192, and DeepSpeed ZeRO-2. Each run takes roughly four hours on 8 NVIDIA H20 80 GB GPUs. Evaluation Protocol and Metrics. We evaluate four capability groups with lmms-eval [ 54 ] under identical settings for all models. General ability is measured on GQA [ 15 ] , VQA-v2 [ 11 ] , and OK-VQA [ 32 ] , and reasoning on ScienceQA [ 30 ] , AI2D [ 20 ] , and POPE [ 23 ] , the last of which probes object-hallucination reasoning. OCR ability is measured on TextVQA [ 39 ] , DocVQA [ 34 ] , and OCRBench [ 29 ] , and grounding on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ [ 19 , 53 ] , and RefCOCOg [ 31 ] . We report ANLS for DocVQA and Acc@0.5 for grounding, where RefCOCO and RefCOCO+ are averaged over testA and testB and RefCOCOg uses its test split. All other benchmarks report accuracy. To summarize performance under pruning, we report two retention metrics relative to the dense base model. The retention of a task is the pruned-model score divided by the dense-model score, expressed as a percentage. We first average retention within each group and then across groups. General-Reasoning Retention (GRR) averages the General and Reasoning groups, and All-Task Retention (ATR) averages all four groups. Latency Measurement. All latency measurements use a single NVIDIA A100 GPU with batch size 1, SDPA attention, and the evaluation resolution, where max_pixels is set to 1,605,632 1{,}605{,}632 . We report TTFT, measured with a single generated token, together with its breakdown into the vision encoder, the projector, and the LLM. Each number is averaged over 5,000 5{,}000 TextVQA samples after five warm-up samples. 4 Rescuing Pruning Across Levels and Mechanisms To systematically investigate the effectiveness of post-training across pruning methods, we comprehensively explore three dimensions: the pruning mechanism (dropping vs. merging), the pruning position (encoder, projector, and LLM), and the compression strength ( 40 / 20 / 10 % 40/20/10\% ). To account for dynamic-resolution inputs and reflect the actual computational budget, we use the average visual-token keep ratio per LLM layer as the invariant for all comparisons. Table 1 summarizes the main results under encoder- and projector-level pruning, and Appendices F.1 , F.2 , and F.3 give the full results for each level. 4.1 What Breaks and What Is Restored Figure 3: Training-free vs. post-trained ATR for 36 pruning configurations on two backbones. Color indicates the pruning level and marker size the keep ratio. The dashed line is y = x y=x , vertical stems mark the post-training gain, and the gray line is a linear fit. CAPT improves every configuration in the design space. All 36 36 configurations in Fig. 3 , spanning two backbones, three pruning levels, two mechanisms, and three keep ratios, lie above the diagonal, so the recovery does not depend on a particular pruning setting. The gain also grows with the severity of training-free degradation, and the fitted slopes stay below one, at 0.52 0.52 on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and 0.81 0.81 on LLaVA-OV-1.5-8B. The previous results show that post-training can recover a large fraction of the performance lost to visual-token pruning. Yet aggressively pruned models often remain below the dense reference even after training. This suggests a natural decomposition of the pruning-induced performance gap into two parts: a recoverable component that can be restored through post-training, and a residual component that mainly reflects the information loss inevitably introduced by pruning. We write Δ gap = G recoverable + R res . \Delta_{\mathrm{gap}}=G_{\mathrm{recoverable}}+R_{\mathrm{res}}. (1) The recoverable component requires further attribution. Our post-training uses a small and diverse dataset to adapt the upstream and downstream layers of the pruning operation to the compressed token distribution, thereby mitigating pruning-induced mismatches such as the attention gap. However, introducing post-training data inevitably brings an additional source of performance gain that is independent of pruning adaptation. We therefore further decompose the recoverable gain into a data gain and an adaptation gain : G recoverable = G data + G adapt . G_{\mathrm{recoverable}}=G_{\mathrm{data}}+G_{\mathrm{adapt}}. Having established that post-training substantially improves the tolerance of MLLMs to aggressive visual-token pruning, we ask how much prefill speedup can be achieved while general understanding and reasoning remain essentially lossless. Under the latency setting of Section 3 , dense Qwen2.5-VL-7B takes 213.06 213.06 ms TTFT per sample, of which the vision encoder accounts for 120.43 120.43 ms, the projector for 0.65 0.65 ms, and the LLM for 85.10 85.10 ms. The projector itself is almost free, yet it is a natural compression point, because pruning there shortens the visual sequence processed by the entire LLM. Projector-level pruning also preserves quality at aggressive budgets. Joint pruning across levels is therefore worthwhile for real acceleration, and CAPT is what rescues the quality of such aggressive joint configurations. 6 Conclusion This paper revisits visual token compression in multimodal large language models from the perspective of post-training. We point out that the performance degradation after pruning stems not only from unrecoverable information loss, but also from the adaptation gap between compressed visual tokens and the original dense-token distribution. To this end, we establish a unified compression-aware post-training framework and systematically analyze the recovery behavior of different compression mechanisms at the encoder, projector, and LLM levels. Our framework achieves significant and comprehensive performance recovery across diverse pruning settings, suggesting that a substantial portion of the degradation caused by training-free pruning is adaptable. Furthermore, we explore aggressive joint pruning across levels, which, with compression-aware post-training, attains the highest speedup among nearly lossless configurations. References [1] S. R.
